VIDEO.title: The SHOCKING Words of Jesus No One Wanted To Hear
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: Whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 16:21-28. From that time Jesus begins to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things, be killed, and be raised on the third day. Peter takes Him aside and rebukes Him; Jesus answers, 'Get behind Me, Satan!' Then He teaches that anyone who wants to come after Him must deny himself, take up his cross and follow Him, for the Son of Man will come and repay each one according to his deeds.

This is the first time Jesus openly discusses His death and resurrection, hence Peter's strong reaction. The last place named is Caesarea Philippi (16:13), so they are probably still there; the video believes the transfiguration that follows took place on Mount Hermon. The leaders of 16:21 together stand for the Sanhedrin.
A few verses after being called Petros, Peter is a skandalon, a stumbling block. Jesus uses the same command He used to Satan in 4:10. Human thinking can unknowingly align with satanic purposes.

Mark says Jesus called the crowd as well (Mark 8:34). Taking up the cross is a continuing act (Luke 9:23, 'daily'). Two treasures are set side by side (6:19-21; 10:38-39), and the promise to repay recalls Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12, a comfort to those who give up the world's riches.
The lesson: fans of Jesus seek comfort over a cross; followers of Jesus seek the cross over comfort. The crowds of John 6 eventually left; followers remain.
QUOTES: Fans of Jesus seek comfort over a cross. Followers of Jesus seek the cross over comfort.
He was Petros. Now he's skandalon.
It is possible for human thinking to unknowingly align with satanic purposes.

LSB_QUOTES.text: From that time Jesus began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem, and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised up on the third day.
Then Jesus said to His disciples, “If anyone wishes to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross and follow Me.
For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?

src.text: From that time Jesus began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem, and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised up on the third day.

lines.text: This is the first time Jesus openly discusses His death and resurrection with His disciples. Jesus has spent much time outside Judea and Jerusalem, and He knows that when He returns the religious leaders will kill Him.
Elders, chief priests and scribes together are an all-encompassing term for the Jewish leaders, the Sanhedrin, the supreme legislative body of the Jewish people.
He had hinted before: the bridegroom 'taken away' (9:15) and the sign of Jonah (12:40).

src.text: And Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him, saying, “God forbid it, Lord! This shall never happen to You.”

lines.text: The disciples seem to have missed the part about being raised. Peter's immediate emotional outburst suggests they heard only suffering and death and stopped listening.

left.text: And I also say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build My church; and the gates of Hades will not overpower it.

right.text: But He turned and said to Peter, “Get behind Me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to Me; for you are not setting your mind on God’s interests, but man’s.”

lines.text: In just a few verses Peter goes from Petros, a rock to build on, to skandalon, another kind of rock: a stone to trip over.
This is not long after Jesus commended him for insight that came from God. 'We should all chew on that one.'

left.text: Then Jesus *said to him, “Go, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve Him only.’”

right.text: But He turned and said to Peter, “Get behind Me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to Me; for you are not setting your mind on God’s interests, but man’s.”

lines.text: Jesus uses the same verb He used to command Satan to be gone. Avoiding the cross is antithetical to God's plan, direct opposition to God.
Ask Peter whether he wanted to serve Satan's purposes and he would say, 'Absolutely not.' Yet human thinking can unknowingly align with satanic purposes.

src.text: And He summoned the crowd with His disciples, and said to them, “If anyone wishes to come after Me, he must deny himself, and take up his cross and follow Me.

lines.text: Mark shows the disciples were not the only ones listening. The invitation is open to anyone with ears to hear.
It is unclear where the crowd came from: perhaps Bethsaida, where Jesus healed a blind man (Mark 8:22-26), or nearer the Decapolis and the four thousand.

left.text: Then Jesus said to His disciples, “If anyone wishes to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross and follow Me.

right.text: And He was saying to them all, “If anyone wishes to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily and follow Me.

lines.text: Carrying one's cross is not a one-time event but a continuing act of the disciple. Luke captures this more obviously with 'daily.'
To deny oneself means to renounce one's own desires, status and self-interest, to seek Jesus' ways over one's own comfort.

left.text: For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?

right.text: But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

lines.text: Pursuing the world's treasure costs your soul and disappears with the world; pursuing God's treasure preserves your soul, with heavenly and everlasting rewards.
This is a rehash of Matthew 6:19-21, and Jesus has said it before: 'And he who does not take his cross and follow after Me is not worthy of Me' (Matthew 10:38).

Fans of Jesus seek comfort over a cross. Followers of Jesus seek the cross over comfort. Fans refuse to deny self; followers want to be like their rabbi and are fully committed to the adventure of walking after Him.
Fans may say amen loudly, admire His miracles and even study Him. Followers do all that, but they also sacrifice and suffer, because Jesus' destiny is their destiny.

left.text: For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of His Father with His angels, and will then repay each one according to his deeds.

right.text: And that to You, O Lord, belongs lovingkindness, / For You repay a man according to his work.

lines.text: Jesus' promise is connected to Psalm 62:12, and Proverbs 24:12 restates it: 'And will not He render to man according to his work?'

REPAY.title: Do not set your heart on riches

src.text: Do not trust in oppression / And do not put vain hope in robbery; / If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them.

lines.text: In Psalm 62 David is fed up with the corruption and deception of mankind. The world's wealth is corrupt and fleeting; God's reward is eternal life and a refuge.
Jesus tracks David's argument when He asks what it profits a man to gain the whole world (16:26).

REPAY.title: A promise to those who give up comfort

lines.text: We often hear 'He will repay' as a scary threat to evildoers. That is entailed, the video says, but here it is a comfort: to those who choose the cross over comfort, Jesus promises to repay them.
Chrysostom read it the same way: after alarming them, 'He comforts them also by His good things.'

left.text: Jesus answered them and said, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you seek Me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.

right.text: As a result of this many of His disciples went away and were not walking with Him anymore.

lines.text: We know why the crowds came: miracles and food. Shortly afterward many left because He told them things they did not want to hear.
Fans follow self, and the self refuses anything that challenges its own sovereignty and comfort.

TERMS.def: Jesus foretelling His suffering, death and resurrection (16:21; 17:22-23; 20:18-19).
The supreme council of the Jewish people in Jerusalem; the video's summary of 'elders and chief priests and scribes.'
Greek skandalon, a trap or obstacle that trips someone. The captions write 'Scandalon.'
To renounce or disown one's own desires, status and self-interest.
To accept a path of shame and death for Jesus' sake, as a continuing way of life.
The video's contrast between admirers who seek comfort and disciples who choose the cross.

WORDS.gloss: It is necessary, must: divine necessity.
To go away, depart; 'Go!' or 'Get behind!'
Stumbling block, trap. Look up: BDAG, σκάνδαλον.
To think, set one's mind on.
To deny, disown utterly; the word used of Peter's denial (26:34).
Life, soul, self. The same word is 'life' in 16:25 and 'soul' in 16:26.
To repay, make good; related to shalom. Look up: BDB or HALOT, שׁלם.

BACKGROUND.p: Rome crucified rebels, slaves and bandits along roads as a public warning. The condemned often carried the crossbeam to the place of execution. 'Take up his cross' would have sounded shocking and shameful, not merely sentimental.
The council in Jerusalem was led by the high priest and included chief priests, elders and scribes. Under Rome it handled religious and many civil matters; it is the body that tries Jesus (26:59).
A psalm of David about waiting silently for God alone, 'my rock and my salvation' (Psalm 62:2). It warns that men of low and high degree are only a breath, and that riches deserve no trust.

WITNESSES.text: For indeed it was a desire of the adversary that Christ should not suffer.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 54, on 16:23. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: Therefore He said not, Let him renounce himself unto death, but, Let him take up his cross; setting forth the reproachful death; and that not once, nor twice, but throughout all life one ought so to do.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 55, on 16:24. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: Having alarmed them therefore hereby, He comforts them also by His good things.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 55, on 16:27. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

DEBATES.p: 16:28 has been read of the transfiguration that follows (Chrysostom), of the resurrection and Pentecost, or of the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70.
Caesarea Philippi is the last place named, so many place this scene nearby. Matthew does not say, and Mark adds a crowd (Mark 8:34).
The video stresses comfort for those who lose their lives for Christ. Many readers also hear a warning of judgment; both sit in 16:25-27.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video lists 'elders and scribes and Pharisees' in 16:21. The verse names 'the elders and chief priests and scribes'; Pharisees are not mentioned.
Peter's rebuke is in verse 22, not verse 23 as said once; verse 23 is Jesus' answer.
On tenses: in 16:24 'take up' is an aorist imperative and 'follow' a present imperative. The continuing sense is clearest in Luke's 'daily' (Luke 9:23).
'The first time' is best taken as the first plain statement; Jesus had hinted at His death before (9:15; 12:40).
That the transfiguration happened on Mount Hermon is the video's view; Mount Tabor is the older tradition, and the Gospels do not name the mountain.
The captions write 'Bethida' for Bethsaida, 'decapus' for Decapolis, and 'Scandalon' for skandalon.

QUESTIONS: Why do you think Peter heard 'killed' but not 'raised up on the third day'?
Peter meant well. Where might your good intentions be setting your mind on man's interests, not God's?
What does 'take up your cross' look like for you this week, not just once but daily?
Which treasure are you tempted to gain at the cost of your soul?
Do you hear 'He will repay' as a threat or a comfort? Why?
Be honest: in what ways are you more fan than follower?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson, stated plainly: fans of Jesus seek comfort over a cross; followers of Jesus seek the cross over comfort. Fans of Jesus refuse to deny self; denying the self is a deal breaker for them. Followers desire to be like their rabbi, their Lord and Savior, and are fully committed to the adventure of walking after Him, with denying the self as its fundamental part. Fans hear Him preach and say amen, wave their hands, marvel at His miracles, and may even study Him; followers do all that, but they also sacrifice and suffer, because Jesus' destiny is their destiny. The crowds eventually disappeared, because fans follow self. To those who choose the cross over comfort, Jesus promises to repay them.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): pray Psalm 62:5-8 slowly, then write down one comfort you are holding onto more tightly than Jesus. Name one small, concrete way to 'deny yourself' in that area this week.

   (video) Elders, chief priests and scribes together are an all-encompassing term for the Jewish leaders, the Sanhedrin, the supreme legislative body of the Jewish people.
   [Background] He had hinted before: the bridegroom 'taken away' (9:15) and the sign of Jonah (12:40). (Matthew 9:15; Matthew 12:40)

   Outburst Matthew 16:22: "And Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him, saying, “God forbid it, Lord! This shall never happen to You.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+16:22

   (video) Fans follow self, and the self refuses anything that challenges its own sovereignty and comfort.

## Key people
- Simon Peter: Rebukes Jesus and is called Satan and a stumbling block. [Background] Later Peter writes that Christ suffered, 'leaving you an example' (1 Peter 2:21).
- Elders, chief priests and scribes: Together, the whole leadership, the Sanhedrin. [Background] They will meet at Caiaphas' house to plot His death (26:3-4).
- The crowd: Called with the disciples to hear the cost (Mark 8:34); fans who will eventually leave. [Background] John 6 records many disciples turning back.
- David: In Psalm 62, fed up with corruption, he trusts God who repays. [Background] Psalm 62 is headed 'A Psalm of David.'

## Places [Background]
- Caesarea Philippi (named in the video): The last place named (16:13); probably where this teaching happens.
- Mount Hermon (named in the video): Where the video believes the transfiguration took place.
- Bethsaida (named in the video): One guess for where the crowd came from (Mark 8:22-26). The captions write 'Bethida.'
- Jerusalem (named in the video): Where He must go to suffer (16:21).

## Key terms
- Passion prediction: Jesus foretelling His suffering, death and resurrection (16:21; 17:22-23; 20:18-19). [Background]
- Sanhedrin: The supreme council of the Jewish people in Jerusalem; the video's summary of 'elders and chief priests and scribes.'
- Stumbling block: Greek skandalon, a trap or obstacle that trips someone. The captions write 'Scandalon.'
- Deny himself: To renounce or disown one's own desires, status and self-interest.
- Take up his cross: To accept a path of shame and death for Jesus' sake, as a continuing way of life.
- Fans and followers: The video's contrast between admirers who seek comfort and disciples who choose the cross.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Crucifixion in Roman Judea: Rome crucified rebels, slaves and bandits along roads as a public warning. The condemned often carried the crossbeam to the place of execution. 'Take up his cross' would have sounded shocking and shameful, not merely sentimental.
- The Sanhedrin: The council in Jerusalem was led by the high priest and included chief priests, elders and scribes. Under Rome it handled religious and many civil matters; it is the body that tries Jesus (26:59).
- Psalm 62: A psalm of David about waiting silently for God alone, 'my rock and my salvation' (Psalm 62:2). It warns that men of low and high degree are only a breath, and that riches deserve no trust.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For indeed it was a desire of the adversary that Christ should not suffer." Homilies on Matthew 54, on 16:23. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Therefore He said not, Let him renounce himself unto death, but, Let him take up his cross; setting forth the reproachful death; and that not once, nor twice, but throughout all life one ought so to do." Homilies on Matthew 55, on 16:24. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Having alarmed them therefore hereby, He comforts them also by His good things." Homilies on Matthew 55, on 16:27. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Who will 'not taste death'? 16:28 has been read of the transfiguration that follows (Chrysostom), of the resurrection and Pentecost, or of the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70.
- Where was this said? Caesarea Philippi is the last place named, so many place this scene nearby. Matthew does not say, and Mark adds a crowd (Mark 8:34).
- Repay: threat or comfort? The video stresses comfort for those who lose their lives for Christ. Many readers also hear a warning of judgment; both sit in 16:25-27.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video lists 'elders and scribes and Pharisees' in 16:21. The verse names 'the elders and chief priests and scribes'; Pharisees are not mentioned.
- Peter's rebuke is in verse 22, not verse 23 as said once; verse 23 is Jesus' answer.
- 'Matthew 16:4' and '16:4-28' are slips for 16:24 and 16:24-28.
- On tenses: in 16:24 'take up' is an aorist imperative and 'follow' a present imperative. The continuing sense is clearest in Luke's 'daily' (Luke 9:23).
- 'The first time' is best taken as the first plain statement; Jesus had hinted at His death before (9:15; 12:40).
- That the transfiguration happened on Mount Hermon is the video's view; Mount Tabor is the older tradition, and the Gospels do not name the mountain.
- The captions write 'Bethida' for Bethsaida, 'decapus' for Decapolis, and 'Scandalon' for skandalon.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why do you think Peter heard 'killed' but not 'raised up on the third day'?
2. Peter meant well. Where might your good intentions be setting your mind on man's interests, not God's?
3. What does 'take up your cross' look like for you this week, not just once but daily?
4. Which treasure are you tempted to gain at the cost of your soul?
5. Do you hear 'He will repay' as a threat or a comfort? Why?
6. Be honest: in what ways are you more fan than follower?

## Application
- (video) The lesson, stated plainly: fans of Jesus seek comfort over a cross; followers of Jesus seek the cross over comfort. Fans of Jesus refuse to deny self; denying the self is a deal breaker for them. Followers desire to be like their rabbi, their Lord and Savior, and are fully committed to the adventure of walking after Him, with denying the self as its fundamental part. Fans hear Him preach and say amen, wave their hands, marvel at His miracles, and may even study Him; followers do all that, but they also sacrifice and suffer, because Jesus' destiny is their destiny. The crowds eventually disappeared, because fans follow self. To those who choose the cross over comfort, Jesus promises to repay them.
- Study note (added): pray Psalm 62:5-8 slowly, then write down one comfort you are holding onto more tightly than Jesus. Name one small, concrete way to 'deny yourself' in that area this week.
